Beginner workout plan

Beginner Full Body Workout

Three sessions a week, every major muscle trained each time, and a simple rule for adding weight. This is the plan to run for your first three months in the gym, before you need anything more complicated.

By Khushi Gupta · Reviewed October 2026 · 5 min read

Who this plan is for

This plan is for anyone with less than about six months of consistent lifting. That includes complete beginners, people coming back after a long break, and anyone who has trained for years without a plan and never really learned the barbell lifts.

Full body training suits beginners for a simple reason: you get better at a movement by practising it often. Squatting, pressing and pulling three times a week gives you three chances to groove the technique, and each muscle gets a growth signal every 48 hours or so instead of once a week.

Three sessions also fits into real life. Monday, Wednesday and Friday is the classic layout, but any three non-consecutive days work. If you miss a session, do it the next day and carry on. Do not try to cram two sessions into one.

How to progress week to week

Progress is the whole point of a plan. The method here is called double progression, and it is the simplest system that actually works.

  1. Each exercise has a target number of reps, for example 3 sets of 8.
  2. Start with a weight you can lift for all sets with two or three reps left in the tank.
  3. When you hit every rep of every set with good form, add weight next session: 2.5 kg (5 lb) on upper body lifts, 5 kg (10 lb) on squats and deadlifts.
  4. If you miss reps, keep the same weight and try again next time.
  5. If you fail the same weight three sessions in a row, drop it by 10% and build back up.

On small exercises such as curls, lunges and dips, add reps before weight. Work from the bottom of the rep range to the top (for example 10 up to 15), then add the smallest weight jump available and start again at 10.

Expect to add weight to most lifts most weeks for the first two months. That pace slows naturally. When jumps stall even after a reset, you have earned an intermediate plan such as the upper/lower split.

Write every set down. A notebook or phone note with the date, weight and reps is the single best predictor of whether a beginner keeps progressing.

Warm-up

Spend 8 to 10 minutes warming up. You are not trying to get tired, only warm and practised.

  • 3 to 5 minutes of easy cardio: bike, rower or brisk incline walk.
  • A few bodyweight squats, lunges and arm circles.
  • Ramp-up sets on the first lift: the empty bar for 10 reps, then about 50% of your work weight for 5, then about 75% for 3, then start your work sets.

Later exercises in the session need only one light set, since your body is already warm by then.

How to pick your starting weights

Start lighter than your ego wants. A first week that feels too easy is perfect, because it leaves room to add weight for weeks before you stall.

If you have never lifted, begin with the empty barbell (usually 20 kg / 45 lb) on squats, bench and overhead press, and a light dumbbell or machine weight elsewhere. Your first few sessions are for learning the movement patterns on the squat and deadlift.

If you have some experience, do a set of 5 to 8 with a challenging weight, plug it into the one rep max calculator, and start your work sets at around 65 to 70% of the estimate. Loading a bar to an exact weight is easy with the plate calculator.

Eating to support the plan

Beginners can build muscle and lose some fat at the same time, but only if they eat enough protein. Aim for roughly 1.6 to 2.2 g of protein per kg of bodyweight (0.7 to 1 g per lb). The protein calculator gives you a daily target.

Calories depend on your goal. To gain muscle as fast as possible, eat a small surplus of 200 to 300 kcal above maintenance. To lose fat while learning to lift, eat 300 to 500 kcal below. Find your maintenance number with the TDEE calculator.

Sleep matters as much as food. Seven to nine hours is where recovery and strength gains happen; see sleep and muscle growth.

When to take a deload

Most beginners do not need a planned deload in the first eight weeks. The weights are light enough that recovery keeps up.

From week 8 onward, take an easier week if your joints ache, your sleep gets worse or several lifts stall at once. Keep the same exercises, use about 60% of your normal weights and cut the sets in half. Then pick up where you left off.

Exercise swaps

If equipment is busy or a movement does not suit you, swap it for something that trains the same pattern:

Planned exerciseGood swap
Barbell back squatGoblet squat or leg press
Bench pressDumbbell bench press or push-ups
DeadliftTrap bar deadlift or Romanian deadlift
Pull-upLat pulldown or assisted pull-up machine
Barbell rowSeated cable row or one-arm dumbbell row
Overhead pressSeated dumbbell shoulder press

Keep the swap for at least four weeks so you can track progress on it. New to the gym in general? Read the beginner gym guide first.

Common beginner mistakes

Most beginners who stall in the first three months make one of a handful of predictable errors. Avoid these and the plan will carry you a long way.

  • Program hopping. Switching plans every two weeks resets progress. Give this one at least 12 weeks.
  • Adding weight with worse form. A rep only counts if it looks like the last one. Shorter range of motion is not progress.
  • Skipping the legs. Squats, deadlifts and lunges train the largest muscles you have and drive most of your strength gains.
  • Resting too little. Two to three minutes between heavy sets is normal. Rushing makes later sets weaker.
  • Undereating protein. Training without enough protein leaves muscle on the table.

Film a set from the side every couple of weeks. Comparing videos with the technique notes on each exercise page, such as the bench press, is the fastest way to fix form without a coach.

Frequently asked questions

How long should I run a beginner full body plan?

Run it for as long as you can keep adding weight, which for most people is three to six months. Move to a split when progress stalls even after resetting the weights.

Can I add extra exercises?

You can add a couple of sets of arm or calf work at the end, but resist adding more. Beginners progress fastest on a short list of big lifts done well, and extra volume mostly adds fatigue.

Is 3 days a week enough to build muscle?

Yes. Training each muscle three times a week with a few hard sets is plenty for a beginner. Consistency over months matters far more than the number of days.

What if I cannot do a pull-up yet?

Use an assisted pull-up machine, a resistance band or the lat pulldown. Add slow negatives, lowering yourself from the top for three to five seconds, to build toward your first full rep.
